name: Child Protection & Education
tagline: Safe children. Quality education. Brighter futures.
summary: Keeping every child safe, enrolled and learning, with families, teachers and traditional leaders working together.

articles.title: Every child belongs in a classroom
articles.pull_quote: A school is only as strong as the village that stands behind it.
articles.body:
In many communities across Northern Ghana, a child’s path to the classroom is longer than the distance on a map. Long walks, school costs, farm and household duties, and early marriage all pull children away from their lessons, and girls are often the first to leave.

NCRI-Ghana’s work starts where those barriers start. We plan to sit with parents, teachers, school management committees and traditional leaders to find out what keeps children out of school in each community, and to agree on practical steps that families can own.

That can mean help with learning materials, remedial reading support, and mentoring for pupils at risk of dropping out. It also means making school a place families trust, with teachers who are supported and learning spaces that are clean, safe and welcoming.

The aim is simple to say and hard to achieve: every child enrolled, attending, and learning to read with confidence, so that education becomes the ordinary expectation in every household.

articles.title: A child is everyone’s child
articles.pull_quote: Protection works when the whole community watches over the child.
articles.body:
Children grow up safer when adults around them know the signs of harm and know exactly where to turn. Violence, neglect, child labour and early marriage are rarely hidden from a close-knit community, but they are often left unspoken.

We aim to work with community members to form child protection groups that listen, raise awareness and refer concerns to the right services, such as district social welfare officers, health workers and the police. Teachers and parents learn together what safe discipline and safe reporting look like.

Children themselves have a voice in this. Clubs and safe conversations give them a way to say what worries them, and to learn their rights in language they understand.

A protective community is not built by one training. It grows from steady conversations, clear steps to follow, and the confidence that when someone speaks up, someone acts.

articles.title: Learning that lasts beyond the school gate
articles.pull_quote: Reading at home turns a lesson into a habit.
articles.body:
Learning does not stop when the bell rings. A child who is read to, who can borrow a book, and who has a quiet corner and a little light in the evening, learns faster and stays in school longer.

NCRI-Ghana is designing simple, low-cost approaches that bring learning into the village: reading circles, community story hours, and take-home materials that parents can use even if they did not have the chance to attend school themselves.

We also care about the practical details that keep girls in class, such as safe and private sanitation, support with menstrual hygiene, and flexible help for children who have missed time.

Small, steady supports like these add up. They turn schooling from a hurdle into a path, and give each child a stronger start.

name: Women & Girls’ Empowerment
summary: Savings, skills, leadership and safety so women and girls can earn, speak and lead.

articles.title: Strong women, thriving communities
articles.pull_quote: When a woman earns, her whole family eats, learns and grows.
articles.body:
Across Northern Ghana, women farm, trade, process food and carry most of the work of the home, often without the savings, credit or training that would let their efforts grow.

We plan to support women’s groups to save together, lend to one another and start or expand small businesses. Village savings and loan groups are simple and run by the women themselves, which makes them durable.

Alongside savings, we offer practical training in record-keeping, pricing and marketing, and link groups to local markets and service providers.

The result we hope for is not just more income, but more say in how money is used, which strengthens households, schools and the wider community.

articles.title: Voices that are heard
articles.pull_quote: Decisions made without women are decisions made with half the knowledge.
articles.body:
In many places, community meetings still happen without women at the table, or with women present but silent. That leaves out the people who often know the most about water, food, health and children.

NCRI-Ghana will work with women, men and traditional leaders to open real space for participation, through leadership training, mentoring and support to stand for roles on school committees, farmer groups and local structures.

Girls matter here too. Clubs and mentors help adolescent girls build confidence, speak in public and imagine futures that were once out of reach.

When women lead, communities tend to notice what had been overlooked. Our job is to help make that leadership possible, and welcome.

articles.title: Free from violence, free to flourish
articles.pull_quote: Safety is the ground every other opportunity grows from.
articles.body:
Violence and harmful practices hold back girls and women more than almost anything else. They end schooling early, damage health, and silence ambition.

We approach this carefully and together. We aim to work with chiefs, elders, faith leaders, men and boys, because lasting change comes when the whole community agrees what is right.

Safe spaces, community dialogue and clear referral routes to health, legal and social services help survivors find support and help prevent harm in the first place.

Every girl deserves to learn, grow and live without fear. Our work is to make that the everyday reality in the communities we serve.

name: Agriculture, Food Security & Rural Livelihoods
tagline: Productive farms. Food security. Increased incomes.
summary: Climate-smart farming, better markets and dry-season water for stronger harvests and incomes.

articles.title: Farming with the weather, not against it
articles.pull_quote: A farmer who can read the season can feed a family through the year.
articles.body:
Smallholder farmers in Northern Ghana grow maize, millet, sorghum, groundnuts, soybean and more, mostly on rain-fed land. When rains come late, stop early or arrive all at once, a whole season’s work is at risk.

NCRI-Ghana will promote climate-smart practices that fit local conditions: improved and drought-tolerant seed, soil and water conservation, mulching, crop rotation and better timing of planting.

Farmer groups and demonstration plots let neighbours learn from neighbours, which is how new methods spread fastest and are adapted to each community.

The goal is productive farms that keep producing in a changing climate, so families can count on food, not hope for it.

articles.title: From harvest to income
articles.pull_quote: A good harvest only helps if it can be stored, sold and sold well.
articles.body:
Many farming families lose part of their harvest to poor storage and sell at the lowest price, right after harvest, when everyone else is selling too.

We aim to help farmers improve storage, group together to sell in bulk, and understand prices and buyers. Simple processing and added-value activities, including those centred on women, can raise incomes further.

Farmer groups, savings and small business training help families turn farm production into steady earnings and invest in their children’s schooling and health.

Food security and income go hand in hand. When both improve, households can face a poor season without going hungry.

articles.title: Water for the dry season
articles.pull_quote: Green rows in the dry months change what a family can plan for.
articles.body:
For months each year the rains are gone and the fields lie bare. Where there is water, families can keep growing vegetables and earning income when little else is possible.

NCRI-Ghana will explore small, community-managed solutions such as protected wells, simple irrigation, water harvesting and dry-season gardens, matched to each community’s needs and resources.

Women and young people often lead this kind of work. With seed, training and a reliable source of water, a small plot can add nutrition to the family meal and cash to the household.

Water is where food security, health and opportunity meet, and where small investments make a visible difference.

name: Youth Development, Skills & Employment
tagline: Skilled youth. Decent jobs. Greater opportunities.
summary: Practical skills, mentoring and pathways into decent work for young people close to home.

articles.title: Skills that earn a living
articles.pull_quote: A skill in the hand is a future close to home.
articles.body:
Young people are Northern Ghana’s greatest asset, yet many leave school without a clear route to decent work, and some leave their communities in search of one.

NCRI-Ghana plans to support practical, market-linked skills training, from agriculture and agribusiness to tailoring, welding, construction trades and digital basics, chosen by what local employers and customers actually need.

Training works best when it combines hands-on practice with apprenticeship and mentoring, so each young person leaves with both a skill and a contact.

Girls and young women are encouraged into trades from which they have often been excluded, so opportunity is shared fairly.

articles.title: Ready for work, ready to lead
articles.pull_quote: Confidence and know-how open doors that certificates alone cannot.
articles.body:
Finding work is not only about technical skill. It is about knowing how to present yourself, manage money, work in a team and keep going when the first attempt fails.

We aim to offer life-skills coaching, financial literacy, job-readiness support and links to employers, cooperatives and apprenticeship opportunities in the region.

Mentors from the community, and from the wider NCRI-Ghana network of volunteers and interns, give young people someone to learn from and lean on.

The goal is decent jobs and sustainable livelihoods, so young people can build a future in the place they call home.

articles.title: Young people as makers and innovators
articles.pull_quote: The next local business is already sitting in a classroom.
articles.body:
Young entrepreneurs see problems that others overlook, and have the energy to try new solutions: solar services, mobile phone repair, food processing, poultry, digital marketing and more.

NCRI-Ghana will support youth to develop business ideas, access small start-up support and join savings and enterprise groups that share risks and rewards.

We also hope to open pathways for young people to take part in local decision-making, so their ideas shape the community they will inherit.

Skilled, confident youth are the strongest guarantee of a resilient region.

name: Climate, Governance & Community Resilience
tagline: A safer environment. Stronger, more resilient communities.
summary: Preparedness, tree planting and accountable local governance that communities help shape.

articles.title: A changing climate, a prepared community
articles.pull_quote: Resilience is what lets a community bend with the storm and stand again.
articles.body:
Northern Ghana lives with the extremes: long dry spells, intense heat, and rains that can arrive suddenly and flood fields and roads. For families who depend on farming, each shock can undo years of progress.

NCRI-Ghana aims to help communities understand the risks they face and plan for them together, through community risk mapping, early warning information, and simple preparedness plans that everyone knows.

Climate adaptation also means practical changes in how land, water and livelihoods are managed, so households have more than one way to earn and recover.

A prepared community loses less, recovers faster and keeps moving forward.

articles.title: Trees, land and a safer environment
articles.pull_quote: Every tree planted is a promise to the next generation.
articles.body:
Healthy land is the foundation of rural life. Trees shade homes, hold soil, protect water and provide fruit, fuel and fodder, but bush fires, over-cutting and degraded land put them at risk.

We plan to work with communities on tree planting, protection of water sources, bush fire prevention and the restoration of degraded land, supported by local rules that people have helped to write.

Young people and schools can take a leading role, planting and caring for trees they will see grow.

A safer environment protects farms, wells and homes, and leaves a better inheritance for the children of the community.

articles.title: Accountable local government, shaped by communities
articles.pull_quote: When people take part, public services start to answer to the people they serve.
articles.body:
Strong communities need decisions that reflect their needs. That depends on people knowing how local government works, how budgets are shaped, and how to make their voices count.

NCRI-Ghana will support community participation in district planning, help citizens understand their rights and entitlements, and encourage open dialogue between community members and local officials.

Simple tools such as community scorecards and public meetings help communities track services and raise concerns constructively, and help officials respond.

Participation and transparency build trust. Where trust grows, communities and government can solve problems together.

name: Water, Sanitation & Hygiene (WASH)
tagline: Safe water. Better sanitation. Healthy communities.
summary: Community-led action to improve access to safe drinking water, inclusive sanitation and practical hygiene education.

articles.title: Safe water is the foundation of community health
articles.pull_quote: Reliable access to safe water supports health, learning and livelihoods.
articles.body:
Access to safe and reliable drinking water is essential for healthy, resilient communities. Where water sources are distant, unreliable or unsafe, families can face added burdens that affect children, women, school attendance and daily livelihoods.

NCRI-Ghana aims to work with communities, local authorities and relevant service providers to identify water access priorities, promote safe water handling and storage, and support practical, locally appropriate solutions. Any infrastructure or service activity will require community consultation, technical assessment and appropriate partnerships.

The aim is to help communities strengthen safe water access and local ownership, while encouraging the care and maintenance needed to keep water services reliable over time.

articles.title: Sanitation that protects dignity and health
articles.pull_quote: Sanitation services should be safe, accessible and inclusive for everyone.
articles.body:
Adequate sanitation helps protect health, dignity and the environment. Barriers can be especially difficult for children, older people and persons with disabilities, and for girls and women who need safe, private facilities.

NCRI-Ghana aims to support community-led sanitation awareness, inclusive planning and collaboration with the appropriate local service providers. Activities may include community discussions on safe sanitation, identifying barriers to access and encouraging the responsible use and maintenance of facilities.

Solutions should fit local needs, protect privacy and dignity, and be planned with the people who will use and maintain them.

articles.title: Everyday hygiene, lasting benefits
articles.pull_quote: Small, consistent hygiene practices can make a meaningful difference.
articles.body:
Handwashing with soap, safe food handling, menstrual hygiene and hygienic water storage are practical behaviours that can help reduce preventable illness. Access to information and facilities matters: people need the knowledge, supplies and enabling conditions to practise what they learn.

NCRI-Ghana aims to promote inclusive hygiene education through community engagement and, where appropriate, collaboration with schools, health workers, traditional leaders and local organisations. Messages should be clear, respectful and adapted to local languages and circumstances.

Community feedback and monitoring can help identify what is useful, what barriers remain and how hygiene promotion can improve over time.
